Court of Queen
’
s Bench of Alberta

Citation: R
v. H.M.T., 2004 ABQB 743

Date:

20041008

Docket:

0306 72257-S1

Registry:

Calgary

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

-
and -

H.M.T.

Appellant

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of

Mr. Justice Peter Martin

_______________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The past four years have been very unkind to the appellant, Ms. T. She
became seriously ill and, as a result, was recently convicted of a charge of
assault with a weapon for which a suspended sentence and two years probation
was imposed. She has appealed that sentence and asked that I impose a
conditional discharge instead.

SUMMARY OF CIRCUMSTANCES

[
2
]

The unfortunate circumstances leading to this conviction are as follows.
Ms. T is now 32 years old. She earned two degrees from the University of
Calgary - a Bachelor of Arts degree in Art History and a Bachelor of Science
degree in Chemistry. Following her graduation she worked in a number of
research related positions and has herself published an article on the
interaction of copper, chromate and arsenic in soil. She then became ill with
schizophrenia and her life changed dramatically. As her illness overtook her,
she began to act erratically and unpredictably. She made poor decisions, driven
by paranoid delusions.

[
3
]

On the 4
th
of March, 2004, while at the University of Calgary
Student Union Building, Ms. T. lost her fingernail grip on reality and slipped
into a psychotic episode. She was observed by others at the Student Union
Centre shouting terribly offensive anti-Semitic comments. When Ms. T. noticed
someone following her she drew a knife from her purse and threatened to use it,
if not left alone. She was overpowered and held for the police.

[
4
]

Following her arrest she was directed to undergo a 30 day psychiatric
examination to determine if she was fit to stand trial. At the completion of
that assessment, Dr. Duksta, a highly qualified forensic psychiatrist, advised
the court that Ms. T. was unfit, so the period of psychiatric remand was
extended a further 30 days. During her hospitalization, Ms. T. was given a
regime of anti-psychotic medication. Eventually she regained her composure to
the point that she was able to understand the proceedings and instruct counsel.
She was then declared fit to stand trial.

[
5
]

On her first appearance she pled guilty to the charge but applied for a
conditional discharge, arguing that she was out of her mind at the time of the
offence. In support of that application she relied on the report of Dr. Duksta,
who had been treating her in the interval. Dr. Duksta thoroughly chronicled Ms.
T.’s decline and how her illness, which he described as paranoid schizophrenia,
had completely overtaken her. Remarkably, he found that Ms. T.’s intellectual
ability had collapsed to the point that she now had a “full scale IQ of 79.
This range of score would suggest borderline mental retardation.” In contrast,
and to illustrate Ms. T.’s previous intellectual ability, her counsel reported
that she had earlier studied and mastered such concepts as “atomic absorption
spectroscopy in inductively coupled plasma”.

[
6
]

In terms of her prognosis, Dr. Duksta initially advised that Ms. T.
required ongoing inpatient psychiatric care. To that end he and a psychiatric
colleague certified her as a formal patient under the
Mental Health Act
,
R.S.A. 2000, which had the effect of detaining her in the hospital. Ms. T.’s
condition has since improved and that certification has been allowed to lapse.
Dr. Duksta further advised that from now on Ms. T. must continue to take the
anti-psychotic medication which has been prescribed to her. Without that
medication, her condition would deteriorate and the psychotic episodes would
likely return.

[
7
]       Ms. T. had never before been involved in criminal
activity and has no criminal record of any kind. She is unmarried and has no
dependents. She now lives with her parents who continue to care for her and
support her. She is unemployed and has been for some time. Since the onset of
her illness her employment has involved rather menial jobs which she was not
able to hold for long.

[7]

None of the foregoing information was disputed by the Crown. Still the
Crown opposed the application for conditional discharge because this was “...a
racist act involving threats with a weapon”. The Crown explained that it was
“really the nature of the act more than the nature of this woman” which mitigated
against a conditional discharge. Defence counsel told the court that neither
Ms. T. nor her family had ever expressed  anti-Semitic views before, nor did
they hold such views. Counsel also advised that before her illness Ms. T. had
dated a Jewish man for some time.

[
8
]

The sentencing Judge considered himself bound by the Court of Appeal’s
decision in
R v. McFarlane
(1976),
1976 ALTASCAD 6 (CanLII)
, 55 A.R. 222, to refuse the discharge,
so he imposed instead a suspended sentence for two years with probation. The
probation order required that Ms. T. attend for treatment, take her medication
as directed by her psychiatrist, refrain from carrying weapons, including
knives, and avoid the Student Union Centre at the University of Calgary.

ANALYSIS

[
9
]

I am troubled that Ms. T. entered a guilty plea to this charge rather
than defend it on the basis that she was not criminally responsible – a defence
which was clearly available and on the information before me, was most likely
to succeed. However, I note at the time that Ms. T. entered her plea she was
fit to stand trial – specifically, she was thought to be able to understand the
proceedings and the consequences thereof, and able to instruct counsel.
Further, she was then and is now represented by able counsel, so I assume her
plea was a considered decision made with the full knowledge of the defence
available to her. It may be that she was concerned about being designated not
criminally responsible by reason of mental disorder and preferred to accept
criminal responsibility or a discharge instead. I do not know. However, counsel
has not asked that I revisit the matter of plea. Therefore, on the basis of the
information before me and the disposition I intend to impose, I will not deal
with this issue further.

[
10
]

The Crown argued that I should dismiss this appeal because the sentence
imposed was not demonstrably unfit and therefore entitled to deference. With
great respect, I disagree. Our law does not require those who commit criminal
offences of this nature - offences where no one is injured, committed while the
accused is in a full psychotic state - to be fixed with a criminal record. On
the contrary,
sections 16
and
672
the

Criminal Code
, provide an
elaborate regime which allows those who are legally insane – even if only
temporarily – to avoid criminal sanctions upon being found not criminally
responsible on account of mental disorder. Treatment rather than punishment is
usually the objective in such cases. See also
Winko v. British Columbia(
Forensic Psychiatric Institute )
, (1999),
1999 CanLII 696 (SCC)
, 135 C.C.C. (3d) 220 (S.C.C.).

[
11
]

Even if the offender is found to be criminally responsible, a serious
mental illness has generally attracted a more lenient disposition reflective of
the offender’s diminished responsibility:
R. v. Taylor
(1975),
1975 CanLII 1447 (ON CA)
, 24
C.C.C. 2
d
551 (Ont. C.A.), and
R. v. Moreau
(1992),
1992 CanLII 3313 (QC CA)
, 76 C.C.C.
3
d
181 (Quebec C.A.).

[
12
]

Ms. T. elected not to pursue a
s.16
defence and the Crown did not raise
the issue. That left two options: either the Crown could withdraw the charge in
favour of alternate measures, as recommended by Dr. Duksta, or the appellant
could plead guilty. I expect the latter option was taken with the expectation
or hope that this offence would attract a conditional discharge and in that way
allow her to escape both the designation of being found not criminally
responsible on account of mental disorder as well as the stigma of a criminal
record.

[
13
]

As I read the trial Judge’s reasons for sentence, he was concerned that
the
McFarlane
decision did not allow for the imposition of a conditional
discharge for an offence of violence save in exceptional circumstances. He also
wanted to ensure that the appellant was required by court order to continue to
take her medications for as long as the court could compel her to do so.

[
14
]

I agree that
McFarlane
speaks against a conditional discharge for
offences of violence or those committed with a weapon. However, with great respect,
I disagree that reasoning was intended to apply to a first offenders who are so
mentally ill that they are completely out of touch with reality while plagued
by their demons. In other words, I think this fact situation falls within the
exceptional circumstances contemplated in the
McFarlane
decision.

[
15
]

In this case a discharge was clearly in the best interests of the
appellant and not contrary to the public interest. Further, a discharge would
be consonant with the basic principles of sentencing which require that a fit
sentence be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of
responsibility of the offender. The blameworthiness of this offender was
nominal at best.

[
16
]

In my opinion these circumstances called for the imposition of a conditional
discharge subject to a probation order which, in addition to the compulsory
conditions, compelled the appellant to attend on her physician as required and
take the medication prescribed to her. That will achieve the important
objective of having her continue to take her anti-psychotic medication (to
which she is responsive) and thus greatly reduce, if not eliminate the
likelihood of another psychotic experience and re-offending. In other words,
Ms. T. will understand that she is required by law to take her medication or
risk sanctions for breaching her probation order. In this way, the imposition
of a conditional discharge will carry the same safeguard as the imposition of a
suspended sentence with probation, but spare the appellant a criminal record.

[
17
]

As there is nothing to be gained by also fixing Ms. T. with a criminal
record, I find that a suspended sentence and the accompanying criminal record
was in these circumstances an unfit sentence. Accordingly, I allow the appeal.
I impose instead a discharge, conditional on the appellant completing a two
year term of probation which, in addition to the mandatory conditions,
requires:

i.          that
she remain within the jurisdiction of the court unless written permission to go
outside the jurisdiction is obtained from the court or her probation officer;

ii.          that
she abstain from the consumption of alcohol and other non-prescription drugs;

iii.         that
she abstain from possessing or carrying a weapon, including a knife;

iv.         that
she continue to reside with her parents;

v.         that
she continue to attend her current physician, Dr. McKay, a psychiatrist, and
take all treatment and medication prescribed by him.

[
18
]

The appeal is allowed.

Heard on the 7th day of October,
2004.

at the City of
Calgary, Alberta this 8
th
day of October, 2004.
